source.title: Flavors of Margin: Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent in Homogeneous Neural Networks
source.authors: Nikolaos Tsilivis; Eitan Gronich; Julia Kempe; Gal Vardi

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices and experimental details.
record.tranche_reason: It uses different measurements—algorithm-dependent margins and test accuracy—to examine whether late-stage margin behavior explains generalization in small controlled classification experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's broad claims about natural-label generalization, memorization, width sweeps, architecture comparisons, large batches, dropout, sharpness, and memorized-example removal are background or absent. The reported experiments measure margins and test accuracy in teacher–student and MNIST digit tasks. Rows capture reported margin trends and accuracy outcomes; cited findings from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: Figures 2 and 5 report held-out accuracy for Adam and full-batch GD on matched MNIST digit tasks, bearing narrowly on V4 through a different baseline method. The extracted rows capture margin dynamics instead of these accuracy comparisons. The supplied figure text does not establish the held-out performance ordering.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. Under the stated homogeneity, loss and steepest-flow assumptions, algorithm-dependent soft margins are nondecreasing and normalized trajectory limit points align with KKT points of the corresponding margin problem. This does not guarantee globally maximal margins. The teacher–student experiments suggest that early dynamics matter and late-stage margin changes alone do not explain large generalization benefits.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments measure algorithm-dependent margins and test accuracy in a teacher–student setup and small MNIST digit tasks, rather than testing the versions' memorization, width, architecture, optimizer-generalization, batch, dropout, sharpness, or example-removal claims. The theoretical analysis assumes steepest flow with infinitesimal learning rate on homogeneous networks and exponential-tail loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scale affects eventual margin; algorithm and margin norm differ; Adam trajectories depend on numerical precision ϵ and momentum; the paper notes early-stage dynamics matter for generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: After separation, each steepest-descent algorithm increases its corresponding geometric margin; smaller initialization produces larger eventual margins.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Late-stage geometric margin behavior depends on optimization geometry and initialization.

fits_no_version.finding: Switching GD to CD produces marginal accuracy benefits, while switching to SD gives similar or marginally worse accuracy; larger margins do not consistently accompany better generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Late-stage geometric margin maximization alone does not explain large generalization benefits in this sparse teacher–student task.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam's margin trajectories depend on epsilon and momentum, and Shampoo attains the largest spectral margin in the tested frozen-output-layer network.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive optimizers exhibit distinct late-stage geometric biases in small MNIST tasks.

record.problems: The generalization experiments are limited to a controlled synthetic teacher–student task and small MNIST digit tasks. Key margin and accuracy comparisons are described qualitatively or shown in figures, and uncertainty estimates are not stated. The theorem concerns infinitesimal-step steepest flow, while experiments use finite training runs.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Findings cited from prior work are not included as this paper's own results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and local connectivity.
SGD or momentum-SGD baselines, language benchmarks, systematic tuning budgets, decoupled weight decay, and switching from Adam to SGD. The reported baseline is full-batch GD.
Batch-size effects and compensating training recipes.
Dropout and its interactions with dataset size, augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, generalization gaps, and ranking against other measures.
Removal of memorized training examples versus random removal.

missing.what: Separate held-out accuracy comparisons between Adam configurations and GD on MNIST 3 versus 6 and 2 versus 7. Accuracy curves are reported but omitted from the rows; their ordering and numerical differences cannot be recovered reliably from the supplied figure text, so no V4 verdict is assigned.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, Figure 2 accuracy panel; Appendix D, Figure 5 accuracy panel

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly identifies the conference year as ICLR 2024; the supplied text identifies the earlier conference version as ICLR 2025. No verdict follows from margin differences alone.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization or natural-label generalization comparison.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No controlled comparison of adaptive optimizers versus SGD on held-out performance.

rows.baseline: Full GD runs; exact value not stated
rows.value: Switching GD to CD brings marginal generalization benefits; switching to SD gives similar or marginally worse test accuracy. Full CD runs show larger benefits than GD-to-CD switching.
rows.note: Prose gives qualitative comparisons, not exact accuracy values. The authors state late-stage margin control does not cause large generalization benefits by itself.
rows.check: Switching between GD, coordinate descent and sign descent does not test V4's adaptive-optimizer comparison. The qualitative accuracy finding is correctly summarized; training duration is 10^5 epochs.

rows.measure: Training margin trajectories γ1 and γ2 after perfect training accuracy
rows.value: Margins start increasing after the algorithms reach 100% train accuracy; SD reaches larger γ1 and GD larger γ2. Default Adam initially increases γ1, then decreases it while slowly increasing γ2.
rows.note: This result concerns margin dynamics; train and test accuracies are described as having long converged, without reported accuracy values.
rows.check: This row records margins, not the Adam-versus-GD held-out accuracy shown separately in Figure 2. Margin trajectories cannot establish V4.

rows.check: Epsilon- and momentum-dependent margin trajectories do not establish held-out performance differences. The stage incorrectly says without momentum while the row includes both momentum settings.
